title: Object / Blob Storage
tagline: Where images, video, backups, and big files actually live — and why you never store them in your database.
summary: Object storage (S3), the metadata-DB pattern, presigned uploads.

paragraphs: **Object storage** (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob) stores arbitrary files ('objects') — images, videos, PDFs, backups — as opaque blobs with a key and metadata, in flat 'buckets'. It's designed for virtually unlimited capacity, extreme durability (e.g., '11 nines' — 99.999999999%), and cheap-per-GB storage, accessed over HTTP.

It is *not* a file system (no real directories, no in-place edits — you replace whole objects) and *not* a database (no querying object contents). You get an object by its key. That simplicity is exactly what lets it scale to exabytes.

sections.title: The golden rule: blobs in object storage, pointers in the DB

paragraphs: Never store large binaries inside your primary database — it bloats the DB, blows up backups, kills cache efficiency, and slows every query. Instead, store the file in object storage and keep only a **reference (URL/key) plus metadata** (owner, size, content-type, timestamps) in the database. The DB stays small and fast; the blobs live where storage is cheap and limitless.

blocks.caption: DB holds metadata + the object key; the bytes live in object storage and are served via CDN.

sections.title: Presigned URLs — don't proxy big files through your app

paragraphs: For uploads/downloads of large files, don't stream the bytes through your application servers — it wastes their bandwidth and capacity. Instead, the app generates a short-lived **presigned URL** that grants the client temporary, scoped permission to upload (PUT) or download (GET) directly to/from object storage. The heavy data path bypasses your servers entirely; they only handle the lightweight metadata.

Reads are typically served through a **CDN** in front of the bucket, so popular files are cached at the edge. This combination — presigned direct uploads + CDN-fronted reads + metadata in the DB — is the standard media-handling pattern in designs like Instagram, YouTube, and Dropbox.

blocks.text: Whenever a design involves photos/videos/files, say: 'Store blobs in object storage (S3), keep metadata + the key in the DB, upload via presigned URLs directly to the bucket, and serve reads through a CDN.' That one pattern answers the storage half of many media questions.

cheatsheet: Object storage (S3/GCS) = cheap, near-infinite, highly durable HTTP blob store; not a filesystem or queryable DB.
Golden rule: store blobs in object storage, keep only the key/URL + metadata in your database.
Use presigned URLs so clients upload/download directly to storage — don't proxy big files through app servers.
Serve reads through a CDN in front of the bucket for low latency + offload.
This (presigned upload + metadata DB + CDN reads) is the standard media pattern (Instagram/YouTube/Dropbox).

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you store user-uploaded images directly as BLOBs in your relational database?
questions.hint: Think about DB size, backups, caching, and query performance.
answer: Large binaries bloat the database, which makes backups/restores slow and expensive, wastes the buffer pool/cache on bytes that won't help queries, and increases I/O on every operation that touches those tables — degrading performance for *all* data, not just images. Relational DBs are optimized for structured, queryable rows, not multi-MB blobs.

The right design keeps the DB lean: store images in object storage and keep just the object key/URL and metadata (owner, size, type) in the DB. Object storage is cheaper per GB, effectively unlimited, and far more durable for this purpose — and reads can be offloaded to a CDN.
keyPoints: Blobs bloat DB → slow backups, poor cache use, more I/O
Hurts performance of all queries, not just images
Store blob in object storage, keep key+metadata in DB
followUps: How would you handle deleting an image so the DB row and the object stay in sync?

questions.prompt: Users upload 1 GB videos. Routing them through your app servers maxes out their bandwidth. How do you fix the upload path?
questions.hint: Let the client talk to storage directly, with temporary permission.
answer: Use **presigned (pre-authorized) upload URLs**. The client asks your app for permission to upload; the app returns a short-lived, scoped URL (and any required fields) that lets the client PUT the video bytes *directly* into object storage. Your servers never touch the gigabytes — they only issue the URL and later record metadata, so their bandwidth and capacity are freed.

For very large files, use multipart upload (split into parts, upload in parallel, resume on failure). After upload completes (often signaled by a storage event/webhook), kick off async processing (transcoding, thumbnailing) via a queue, and serve playback through a CDN. This is exactly how large-media platforms handle uploads.
keyPoints: Presigned URLs for direct client→storage upload
App only issues URL + records metadata (no byte proxying)
Async transcode via queue after upload; serve via CDN
followUps: How do you know the upload finished, and how do you trigger transcoding?
